extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate and graduate students (and instructors) studying algebraic topology / homology theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the formal axioms, sequences, and computational tools for singular and cellular homology (Mayer–Vietoris, homology with coefficients, mapping torus sequences, functoriality, etc.) used in algebraic topology. Targets constructing and reasoning about homology theories and computing homology groups of spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris sequence (existence and form)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a pair of subspaces A, B ⊂ X such that X is the union of the interiors of A and B, there is a long exact sequence ... → Hn(A ∩ B) → Hn(A) ⊕ Hn(B) → Hn(X) → Hn−1(A ∩ B) → ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the short exact sequence of chain complexes 0 → Cn(A ∩ B) --ϕ→ Cn(A) ⊕ Cn(B) --ψ→ Cn(A + B) → 0 with ϕ(x) = (x, −x) and ψ(x,y) = x + y; check exactness by verifying Ker ϕ = 0, Im ϕ ⊂ Ker ψ and Ker ψ ⊂ Im ϕ. The boundary map ∂: Hn(X) → Hn−1(A ∩ B) is made explicit by representing a class α by a cycle z = x + y with x in A and y in B and taking ∂α to be the class represented by ∂x = −∂y. Useful for calculations and induction arguments (if a statement holds for A, B, and A ∩ B, it can be deduced for A ∪ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a formally identical Mayer–Vietoris sequence for reduced homology groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by augmenting the short exact sequence of chain complexes in the obvious way; the same exact-sequence machinery applies to reduced chains/groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris for deformation-retract neighborhoods / CW subcomplexes
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are deformation retracts of neighborhoods U and V with U ∩ V deformation retracting onto A ∩ B (for example, subcomplexes of a CW complex with suitable neighborhoods), then the usual Mayer–Vietoris sequence applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the five-lemma to show maps Cn(A + B) → Cn(U + V) induce isomorphisms on homology; neighborhoods Nε(A), Nε(B) with Nε(A) ∩ Nε(B) = Nε(A ∩ B) provide the required hypotheses for CW complexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact sequence for mapping torus / two maps f,g: X → Y
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two maps f,g : X → Y and the quotient space Z formed by identifying (x,0) ∼ f(x) and (x,1) ∼ g(x) in X × I ∐ Y, there is a long exact sequence ... → Hn(X) --(f*−g*)→ Hn(Y) → Hn(Z) → Hn−1(X) --(f*−g*)→ Hn−1(Y) → ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by considering q : (X × I, X × ∂I) → (Z, Y) and the induced map of long exact sequences; the kernel of the inclusion-induced map consists of pairs (α,−α) and q* sends (α,−α) to f*(α) − g*(α). Special cases: if f=g=id then Z = X × S1; if one map is identity, Z is the mapping torus of the other. Use this sequence to compute homology of mapping tori (example: Klein bottle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Mayer–Vietoris sequence (pairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a pair (X, Y) = (A ∪ B, C ∪ D) with C ⊂ A and D ⊂ B and X the union of interiors of A and B (and Y the union of interiors of C and D in Y), there is a relative Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence ... → Hn(A ∩ B, C ∩ D) → Hn(A, C) ⊕ Hn(B, D) → Hn(X, Y) → ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from a commutative diagram of chain complexes where Cn(A + B, C + D) is the quotient of Cn(A + B) by Cn(C + D); view rows as chain complexes and use the short exact sequence of chain complexes to get the long exact sequence of homology groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology with coefficients (definition and general properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define chains Cn(X; G) with coefficients in an abelian group G (chains are finite sums ∑ ni σi with ni ∈ G); boundaries use the same formula so ∂^2 = 0, giving homology groups Hn(X; G) and relative groups Hn(X, A; G). Reduced groups defined via augmented chain complex ... → C0(X;G) →ε G → 0 with ε summing coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All theory for Z coefficients carries over to arbitrary coefficient groups G with no change in proofs; cellular homology generalizes (cellular chain groups become direct sums of G's), and H_CW^n(X;G) ≈ Hn(X;G). Differences between Hn(X;G) and Hn(X;Z) appear mainly in calculations; there is a general algebraic relation expressing Hn(X;G) in terms of Hn(X;Z) (treated later). Homomorphisms φ: G1→G2 induce maps φ_* on homology and commute with f_* induced by maps of spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special case: G = Z2 simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When G = Z2, chains are sums of simplices with coefficients 0 or 1, so one can think of chains as finite 'unions' of simplices; signs disappear and orientation issues are ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Z2-coefficients are often the most natural tool in the absence of orientability; boundary formulas simplify since no signs are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular homology with coefficients and isomorphism to singular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex, the cellular chain group Hn(Xn, Xn−1; G) is a direct sum of copies of G (one per n-cell) and the cellular homology H_CW^n(X;G) agrees with singular homology Hn(X;G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellular boundary maps are given by the same formula as for Z-coefficients and the same proofs apply; one needs to know the cellular incidence numbers d_{αβ} are the same as before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (degree m map acts by multiplication by m)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : S^k → S^k has degree m, then f_* : Hk(S^k; G) → Hk(S^k; G) is multiplication by m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses naturality with respect to a homomorphism φ: Z → G sending 1 to a chosen element g ∈ G and a commutative diagram reducing to the integer-coefficient case where degree action is evident; therefore the induced map sends g to m g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom (1): Homotopy invariance of a homology theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ≃ g : X → Y then f_* = g_* : h_n(X) → h_n(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental invariance property: induced maps depend only on homotopy class. (Stated for reduced homology and CW complexes in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom (2): Long exact sequence for a pair (boundary and naturality)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are boundary homomorphisms ∂: h_n(X/A) → h_{n-1}(A) (or the relative formulation) fitting into a long exact sequence ... → h_n(X/A) --q_*→ h_n(X) --i_*→ h_n(A) --∂→ h_{n-1}(X/A) → ... with naturality under maps of pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axiomatize existence of long exact sequence of the pair with natural boundary maps; in unreduced formulation this is broken into long exact sequence plus excision statements. These exact-sequence axioms underlie constructions like Mayer–Vietoris.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom (3): Wedge-sum (or disjoint-union) axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: For a wedge sum X = ∨_α X_α with inclusions i_α: X_α → X, the direct-sum map ⊕ i_α* : ⊕_α h_n(X_α) → h_n(X) is an isomorphism for each n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite wedge sums this can be deduced from the first two axioms; for infinite wedge sums it is an independent axiom. In unreduced theories the wedge-sum property is replaced by a disjoint-union statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension axiom / normalization (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms there is often a dimension axiom stating that the groups h_n(point) are zero for n ≠ 0 (normalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom normalizes the theory (singular homology satisfies it). Omitting it allows exotic theories (e.g., bordism) where a point has nontrivial groups in infinitely many dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris derivable from homology axioms for CW complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X = A ∪ B with A and B subcomplexes, the axioms imply a Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence ... → h_n(A ∩ B) → h_n(A) ⊕ h_n(B) → h_n(X) → ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the inclusion-induced commutative diagram of exact sequences for pairs (B, A ∩ B) → (X, A) and the algebraic fact (Exercise 38) that such a diagram with every third vertical map an isomorphism yields the long exact sequence involving the remaining terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular homology as a (co)variant functor — functoriality requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular homology assigns to each space X an abelian group Hn(X) and to each map f: X → Y a homomorphism f_*: Hn(X) → Hn(Y) such that (f ◦ g)_* = f_* ◦ g_* and id_* = id; this is the covariant functor property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish covariant functors (like homology) from contravariant ones (like cohomology); functoriality and naturality statements are used throughout (e.g., induced maps commute with coefficient-group homomorphisms and with the boundary maps in long exact sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category and functor formalism prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the language of categories and functors to formalize constructions: a category has objects, morphisms, identity morphisms, and associative composition; a functor assigns objects and morphisms in one category to another preserving identities and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal viewpoint clarifies why homology groups and induced maps behave as they do, and it allows many constructions to be phrased uniformly (e.g., chain complexes form a category, functors preserve structure). Examples: topological spaces category, category of abelian groups, homotopy category, chain-complex category.
